lesson_core_move: Convert $e^{st}$ with $s=j\omega$ into $e^{j\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)+j\sin(\omega t)$ to interpret pure complex exponentials as constant-magnitude rotating phasors rather than growing or decaying signals.

images.section_title: Interpreting $e^{j\omega t}$ as a Rotating Phasor
images.image_description: Textbook-style line art on a white background: draw the complex plane with a labeled real axis and imaginary axis, a unit circle centered at the origin, and a bold phasor arrow from the origin to a point on the circle at angle $\omega t$ measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. Label the angle arc $\omega t$ and keep the arrow length equal to 1. Optionally include a faint second arrow or trail showing an earlier position to suggest counterclockwise rotation as $t$ increases when $\omega>0$.

outline_section.section_title: Interpreting $e^{j\omega t}$ as a Rotating Phasor
outline_section.learning_goal: Interpret $e^{j\omega t}$ as a unit-magnitude phasor that rotates in the complex plane.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean complex-plane diagram with real and imaginary axes, a unit-circle phasor arrow at angle $\omega t$, and optional snapshots showing counterclockwise rotation as $t$ increases.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Textbook-style line art; keep the circle and arrow simple and emphasize unit magnitude and counterclockwise rotation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices describing the phasor motion; choose the single best interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which description best matches the motion of $e^{j\omega t}$ on the complex plane as $t$ increases for $\omega>0$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that describes a fixed point on the complex plane.
Include one choice that reverses the rotation direction.
Include one choice that treats the phasor as a growing spiral.
Include one choice that claims the magnitude changes with time.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use the complex-plane picture to explain how $e^{j\omega t}$ traces a rotating phasor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the real and imaginary parts trace a point on the unit circle with angle $\omega t$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from algebraic expansion to geometric meaning in the complex plane.
solution_step_plan: Read the cosine and sine pair as coordinates.
Place the point on the unit circle.
State the direction of motion for positive $\omega$.
Connect the motion to the phasor idea.
practice_variation_axes: Ask for the direction of rotation.
Ask for the unit-circle location at a specific time.
Ask for the phasor description in words.

outline_section.handoff_notes: This is the only step that should request a diagram; keep the follow-up questions symbolic and centered on rotation, not on growth.
